question: In ECHR case 001-57990 (application no. 19380/92 against the United Kingdom), on what two distinct grounds did the Divisional Court hold that the magistrates' decision to commit the applicant to prison was wrong, and what unusual procedural step did the Chamber take at the ECHR stage?
ground_truth: The Divisional Court held the committal decision wrong on two grounds: (1) the finding of culpable neglect was unsustainable on the evidence — before such a finding could be sustained there would need to be clear evidence that gainful employment for which the applicant was fit had been on offer and refused, but no such evidence existed; (2) even if culpable neglect had been established, a committal order was only to be made if payment could be made and there was no other way of inducing payment, but the applicant had no means at the time of the hearing, so the magistrates were bound to consider the alternatives (suspended imprisonment subject to conditions, or refusing the warrant and waiting for changed circumstances). At the ECHR stage, following its deliberations on 23 November 1995 (the public hearing having been held the previous day, 22 November 1995), the Chamber relinquished jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber under Rule 51 § 1.

question: In ECHR case 001-57899 (application no. 18711/91 against the United Kingdom), what sequence of events led to the applicant being denied legal aid for his criminal appeal, and what was the outcome when he argued the appeal without legal representation?
ground_truth: After conviction, new solicitors briefed counsel who twice stated he lacked sufficient material to assess prospects and ultimately concluded he could not support the appeal; the solicitors accordingly withdrew. The Scottish Legal Aid Board refused legal aid, finding no substantial grounds for appeal and that granting legal aid would not be reasonable. Despite this advice the applicant proceeded alone. On 24 January 1991 he presented the appeal himself before the High Court of Justiciary — with no legal knowledge and no assistance — while the Crown was represented by counsel. The court addressed only the first two grounds (concerning the witness Mrs G.) and found them ill-founded; as the applicant did not address the remaining grounds they were not considered. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed, although the court did examine other points raised by the applicant and concluded there had been no miscarriage of justice.

question: In ECHR case 001-57871 (application no. 14220/88 against Sweden), on what three occasions was the applicant fined for improper statements in court filings, and what legal provision did the courts apply each time?
ground_truth: All three fines were imposed under Chapter 9, Article 5, of the Code of Judicial Procedure, which empowered courts to fine parties for 'improper' statements prejudicing good order in proceedings. First fine — the District Court fined the applicant 1,000 kronor on 18 May 1987 for written observations of 4 May 1987 in which he described members of the Board of the Principal Guardian as a 'basket of municipal rotten eggs' sharing a 'fascist' ideology. Second fine — the Court of Appeal for Western Sweden imposed a further 1,000 kronor fine on 4 November 1987 for his appeal observations of 1 June 1987, in which he described the Supreme Court as 'generally lethargic, lax and allergic' due to 'anti-human rights indoctrination.' Third fine — the same Court of Appeal, in a separate decision of 4 November 1987, imposed an additional 1,000 kronor fine for his appeal of 2 July 1987, in which he described a named judge as having a 'far-reaching tendentiously fascist way of presiding' and alleged 'collegiate corruption and abuse of public power.'

question: In ECHR case 001-57642 (application no. 11581/85 against Sweden), what discriminatory mechanism prevented the applicant from obtaining a reduction of the church tax, and what outcome did the Parliamentary Ombudsman's intervention produce?
ground_truth: The applicant was unable to claim the reduced church tax rate under the Tax (Reduction of Dissenters' Liability) Act 1951 (the Dissenters Tax Act) because that Act required the taxpayer to be formally registered as a resident in Sweden (mantalsskriven). The applicant — a Finnish citizen working in Sweden but living on the Finnish island of Lemland — was not formally registered as a resident, even though he was taxed as one for income purposes and was neither a member of the Church of Sweden, nor a Swedish citizen, nor actually resident there. The Parliamentary Ombudsman, in a decision of 16 April 1982, found the registration requirement inconsistent and without objective justification, and on the same day wrote to the Government proposing its abolition. As a direct result of the Ombudsman's proposal, the Dissenters Tax Act was subsequently amended to remove the formal registration requirement.

question: In ECHR case 001-68178 (application no. 55853/00 against Sweden), what was the substance of the applicant's disability benefits claim and what legal provision did each court level invoke when refusing his repeated requests for an oral hearing?
ground_truth: The applicant sought disability benefits (handikappersättning) under Chapter 9, section 2 of the Social Insurance Act 1962, claiming that before his 65th birthday in 1983 he had incurred extra costs due to Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (diagnosed September 1982). The Social Insurance Office rejected the application finding his disability had not reached the required level before age 65. All three courts refused oral hearings by applying section 9 of the Administrative Court Procedure Act 1971, which allows courts to dispense with oral hearings where they consider them unnecessary: the County Administrative Court found no uncertainty in the medical assessment that could not be clarified in writing; the Administrative Court of Appeal found a hearing unnecessary for determining leave to appeal; and the Supreme Administrative Court noted it did not normally hold oral hearings. At every level the applicant argued Article 6 of the Convention required a hearing, but no court accepted that argument — an analysis presented to the Supreme Administrative Court by its legal secretary opined that the lower court's refusal was not incompatible with the Convention.

question: In ECHR case 001-73360 (application no. 44362/04 against the United Kingdom), what were the Secretary of State's specific policy criteria for granting artificial insemination facilities to prisoners, and on what grounds did the Court of Appeal uphold the refusal?
ground_truth: The Secretary of State's policy granted facilities only in 'exceptional circumstances,' giving particular attention to six factors: (1) whether artificial insemination was the only means by which conception was likely; (2) whether the prisoner's expected release date was neither too near nor so distant as to prevent assuming parental responsibilities; (3) whether both parties and medical authorities consented and confirmed medical fitness; (4) whether the couple had a well-established, stable relationship predating imprisonment that was likely to continue after release; (5) whether domestic circumstances and welfare arrangements for any child were satisfactory; and (6) whether the prisoner's history and public interest considerations militated against the provision. Applying these criteria, the Secretary of State refused the request in his letter of 28 May 2003 on five grounds: the relationship was formed while both were imprisoned and untested in normal life; there was insufficient provision for the child's material welfare; the immediate support network was inadequate; a child would be without a father for an important part of its childhood; and the violence of the crime raised legitimate public concern that the punitive and deterrent elements of the sentence would be circumvented. The Court of Appeal upheld the refusal not by re-enumerating those reasons but by relying on R (Mellor) v. Secretary of State for the Home Department: it held that the policy was rational and otherwise lawful, and that the Secretary of State had neither irrationally misapplied his own policy nor acted disproportionately on the circumstances presented to him.

question: In ECHR case 001-60735 (application no. 38629/97 against Sweden), how did the County Administrative Court and the Administrative Court of Appeal differ in their treatment of the disability benefits claim, and what additional procedural complaint did the applicant raise about the appellate proceedings?
ground_truth: The County Administrative Court gave judgment in the applicant's favour: it found the Social Insurance Office's original 1987 decision had been based on insufficient information, held the Office should have reviewed it at the applicant's request, and granted disability benefits as from July 1986. The Administrative Court of Appeal reversed this by 3 votes to 2, without holding an oral hearing, and confirmed the Office's rejection — finding no basis for a review of the original decision. The dissenting judges would have upheld the disability allowance. Beyond the denial of an oral hearing, the applicant raised an additional procedural complaint: the Administrative Court of Appeal refused to order the National Social Insurance Board to clarify or explain the reasons for its appeal, even though the Board had failed to adequately explain its position. When the applicant posed specific questions to the Board, the court merely forwarded these to the Board rather than compelling a substantive reply. The applicant relied on this failure, together with the refusal to hold a hearing, as grounds for questioning the impartiality of the proceedings.

question: In ECHR case 001-58838 (application no. 33274/96 against the United Kingdom), under what statutory authority was the postal redirection order made, and which specific categories of correspondence were intercepted between the applicant and which institutions?
ground_truth: The postal redirection order was made by the District Judge at Reading County Court under section 371 of the Insolvency Act 1986, on an ex parte application by the Receiver and Trustee in Bankruptcy, on the grounds that the Trustee needed to intercept mail immediately and without notice to the applicant in order to identify his assets and sources of income. Between 27 September 1996 and 10 January 1997, 71 letters were redirected, all copied to file before being forwarded to the applicant. The intercepted correspondence included: a letter from the Chief Inspector of the Ministry of Defence Police; two letters from the Legal Aid Board (concerning civil proceedings to which the applicant was a party); a letter from the Police Complaints Authority; two letters from his legal advisers at the Legal Department of the National Council for Civil Liberties, relating to proceedings before the European Commission of Human Rights; and affidavits and drafts prepared for use in the High Court receivership proceedings. The Trustee subsequently agreed that correspondence from the Police, Legal Aid, the National Council for Civil Liberties, and the European Court of Human Rights would not be opened in future, provided sender names were clearly stamped on envelopes.

question: In ECHR case 001-57901 (application no. 18949/91 against the United Kingdom), what was the sequence of failed legal representation attempts before the appeal hearing, and how did the High Court of Justiciary address the applicant's grounds when he argued the case in person?
ground_truth: After conviction, trial counsel advised there were no grounds for appeal; a first new firm of solicitors also found no basis for appeal and withdrew. A second new firm obtained an adjournment but could find no counsel willing to present the appeal and also withdrew; a third adjournment was granted. A third firm applied for legal aid: freshly consulted counsel concluded there was 'no ground of appeal against conviction and no prospects of appealing successfully against sentence.' The Scottish Legal Aid Board refused legal aid on those grounds; the third firm also withdrew. After yet another adjournment, the applicant argued his own appeal on 21 March 1991 before a three-judge bench presided over by the Lord Justice Clerk — one of the two most senior judges in Scotland — while the Crown was represented by counsel who did not apparently intervene. The Lord Justice Clerk gave detailed consideration to each ground the applicant had formulated himself — including alleged fabricated evidence, false witness testimony, uncalled witnesses, insufficient evidence of permanent disfigurement, and disregard of his instructions by legal advisers — but found none had substance and concluded there had been no miscarriage of justice, dismissing the appeal.

question: In ECHR case 001-58095 (application no. 22410/93 against the United Kingdom), what sequence of procedural delays caused the protracted costs proceedings, and what was the final outcome of the applicants' appeal against the costs order?
ground_truth: The delays arose from multiple causes: (1) on 24 September 1991 the judge adjourned the costs inquiry pending clarification of legal aid issues; (2) the Legal Aid Board's report was not forwarded to the parties until 14 January 1992; (3) a further nine-month delay resulted from the Department of Social Security's erroneous belief that the applicants had separated, causing it to require a fresh means assessment — the DSS later acknowledged this was a misapprehension; (4) after the restored hearing of 12–13 November 1992, the applicants sought legal aid to appeal the costs order but the appeal time-limit had already expired on 11 December 1992; (5) queries in the Civil Appeals Office as to whether leave to appeal was required were not resolved until 10 April 1994; (6) multiple extensions were needed because the applicants could not obtain transcripts and judge's notes — it transpired that the first judge's notes had been either lost or never existed; and (7) transcripts of the second-instance judgment were produced at public expense only in October 1994, and the full documents were lodged on 6 March 1995. The Court of Appeal heard the appeal on 19 June 1995 and confirmed the costs order, dismissing the appeal.
